newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA OPPOSITION WIN PROMPTS GOVT SOUL-SEARCHING.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA OPPOSITION WIN PROMPTS GOVT SOUL-SEARCHING.

text.p: A convincing opposition win in Bulgaria's presidential election prompted the chastened ex-communist government to pledge a thorough policy review.
Although the president has few powers and the Socialist party will remain in government, Prime Minister Zhan Videnov said the party must take note of the electorate's strong message of disapproval.
"We have important, radical and maybe painful decisions to take in the interests of the country," Videnov told reporters.
He said a party congress could be held as early as January and did not rule out cabinet changes.
Videnov called the victory of the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) in the run-off for the presidency "an impressive win" and congratulated its candidate, 44-year-old lawyer Petar Stoyanov.
With a third of polling station returns counted, official results showed Stoyanov leading with 61.21 percent of the vote to Socialist Culture Minister Ivan Marazov's 38.79 percent.
"This is not a tiny majority against, this is an overwhelming vote for," said political analyst Evgenii Dainov of the Centre for Social Practices.
Georgi Bliznashki, a member of the divided Socialists' reformist wing, said pressure for change had come from the grass roots.
"The important thing is to change our style of leadership. We must become more responsive to the public," he said.
As his supporters took to the streets waving blue UDF flags, Stoyanov pledged to bring his country closer to the European Union and NATO.

Stoyanov was careful to avoid direct criticism of the Socialists and proposed a National Salvation Council of experts and respected public figures to advise the government on how to fight the country's deep economic crisis.
"Political independence and economic stability come through integration into the European Union and the Atlantic Alliance," Stoyanov told a news conference.
Bulgaria has the lowest level of foreign investment of the east European former Soviet satellites, and a lingering tendency to seek guidance from Moscow rather than Brussels.
Sunday's vote took place against a background of falling living standards and fears of food and power shortages in the coming Balkan winter.
Even workers in the smokestack industries of the red heartland said they had deserted the Socialists, who won a majority in parliamentary elections in December 1994.
Bombings and other violence have marred Bulgaria's second presidential campaign since the fall of communism in 1989, culminating in the murder last month of former prime minister Andrei Lukanov.
Shortly after voting began, a caller telephoned a bomb threat to a city centre school where President Zhelyu Zhelev was due to cast his ballot. A thorough search found nothing, state radio said.
Zhelev, a pro-market liberal like Stoyanov, lost a U.S.-style primary in June and has not stood for re-election.
The vote coincided with an International Monetary Fund mission discussing terms for release of a delayed $115 million credit vital to stop Bulgaria defaulting on its foreign debt.
